core_findings: Gas & Services is economically dominant but must not be homogenized: Large Industries, Industrial Merchant, Healthcare and Electronics have different contracts, capital intensity, regulation and customer economics.

Large Industries is a dedicated-asset/on-site/pipeline model with contractual energy pass-through; Industrial Merchant is a local distribution/cylinder/service network; Healthcare combines regulated medical gases and homecare; Electronics combines ultra-high-purity consumables, site systems and qualification; E&T is project/technology activity.
H1 2026 reported growth is decomposed into comparable, significant-scope, energy and FX effects. DIG is scope, not organic growth.
E&T group-plus-third-party order intake is not external revenue backlog.
open_uncertainties: E&T internal/external order economics remain incompletely split.
Customer-level concentration is not fully public.
reopen_triggers: Material change to reporting perimeter or business-line definitions.
Evidence that pass-through/perimeter bridges are misclassified.

core_findings: Group and G&S operating margins expanded materially in 2025 and H1 2026 while comparable sales growth remained moderate.
Efficiencies and Industrial Merchant pricing are observable contributors, but exact margin attribution across productivity, price, mix/volume, energy denominator and DIG PPA remains incomplete.
Economic quality is supported by diversified profit pools and high absolute operating margins, not by treating industrial gases as a single commodity business.
open_uncertainties: Durability of the full margin step-up cannot be assigned to one structural lever.
Business-line returns are not separately disclosed.
reopen_triggers: Sustained margin reversal after normalization.
Evidence that recent efficiencies are largely non-repeatable or offset by hidden costs.

core_findings: The strongest moat evidence is local infrastructure/network density, asset specificity and reliability in Large Industries, reinforced by route/cylinder density in merchant distribution and site integration/qualification in Electronics.
Healthcare adds regulatory, logistics and patient-service friction, but reimbursement/tender systems cap monetization.
Long-term contract duration receives no standalone moat credit because Linde and Air Products disclose similar on-site architectures.
Industrial Merchant pricing is segment-specific and does not prove group-wide pricing power.
open_uncertainties: Direct switching/renewal/displacement data are not public.
Route-level merchant cost curves and retention are unavailable.
Electronics dual-source practices by molecule/customer remain incompletely evidenced.
Current China/local-basin shares remain weakly evidenced.
reopen_triggers: Material contract displacement or loss of basin density.
Evidence of worsening merchant retention or route economics.
Loss of semiconductor qualification/site positions.
Regulatory change reducing healthcare service barriers.

core_findings: Runway is supported by multi-year Large Industries/Electronics project starts, advanced semiconductor/HBM capacity, Healthcare patient/service growth and a broad investment opportunity set.
The €6bn investment backlog is a decided-investment measure, not revenue backlog; announced fabs become recurring gas revenue only after commissioning and production ramp.
DIG contributes perimeter growth but no synergy/return uplift is credited before realization.
Hydrogen/CCS is conditional upside with material subsidy, offtake and execution dependencies rather than proven base-case economics.
open_uncertainties: Backlog-to-revenue conversion and project IRRs are not disclosed.
Homecare unit economics by geography are unavailable.
Semiconductor customer concentration and fab utilization remain uncertain.
Energy-transition project returns without support remain unknown.
reopen_triggers: Major project cancellations/delays.
Semiconductor capex or utilization downcycle beyond current assumptions.
Material reimbursement cuts in Healthcare.
DIG integration underperformance.

core_findings: Canonical FY2025 ROIC is bounded around 10.5%-11.0%; recurring issuer ROCE at 11.2% is a corroborating diagnostic, not the canonical measure.
ROIC ex-goodwill is materially higher, showing acquisition goodwill drag, but goodwill is not removed from the primary quality judgment.
Short-period ROIIC is not economically interpretable because DIG, FX/perimeter and long construction lags destabilize the denominator.
Issuer ROCE improved from 2023 through 2025 and remains near that level in H1 2026 despite DIG/construction capital.

Canonical ROIC_TREND is UNCLEAR: FY2025 Standard ROIC is reconstructed, but the locked lineage does not contain a normalized multi-period canonical Standard ROIC series sufficient for a directional state.

R&D-adjusted ROIC is NOT_APPLICABLE: FY2025 R&D of EUR 208m is recurring but does not materially distort comparison against the group revenue, operating-profit and invested-capital base; no capitalization useful-life assumption is introduced.

Overall return economics are INTERPRETABLE_WITH_LIMITATIONS: current canonical ROIC/all-in/ex-goodwill diagnostics are usable, while ROIIC, trend history and acquisition-cohort returns remain constrained.
RETURN_ATTRIBUTABILITY is LOW because Airgas, NovaAir and DIG cohort economics and organic/acquired NOPAT/capital separation are not sufficiently disclosed for clean attribution.
open_uncertainties: Full acquisition-cohort returns for Airgas, NovaAir and DIG are unavailable.
Project-level returns and utilization are not disclosed.
Exact WACC/hurdle comparison belongs to Valuation; CLEARLY_POSITIVE is a qualitative economic-spread judgment, not a WACC calculation.
Normalized canonical Standard ROIC history before FY2025 is not reconstructed in the locked calculation lineage; issuer ROCE history is corroborating only.
reopen_triggers: Sustained ROIC decline below the historical capital-cost buffer.
Evidence of poor returns on current Electronics/LI backlog.
Material acquisition impairment or DIG return shortfall.

roic_trend_judgment.method: Frozen Analysis Standard §9.11: classify ROIC trend from normalized multi-period ROIC history; do not substitute ROIIC or issuer return metrics.
evidence_basis: E-150/E-153: audited inputs supporting FY2025 canonical Standard ROIC
calculation_basis: CALC-ROIC-005 establishes FY2025 canonical Standard ROIC 10.5%-11.0% only
No cutoff-admissible normalized canonical Standard ROIC series exists for multiple full years in the locked calculation lineage
limitations: Issuer ROCE rises through FY2025 and remains near that level in H1 2026, but it is a corroborating diagnostic rather than canonical Standard ROIC.
H1 2026 is interim and distorted by DIG purchase accounting and construction capital.
ROIIC remains NOT_INTERPRETABLE and is not used as a trend substitute.
roic_trend_judgment.judgment_rationale: Directional canonical ROIC trend cannot be established without substituting issuer ROCE for normalized multi-period Standard ROIC; the exact allowed uncertainty state is therefore UNCLEAR.

rd_adjusted_roic_judgment.applicability_basis: Frozen trigger requires material, recurring, multi-period R&D whose expensing materially distorts comparison. Recurrence is present; material distortion is not.

basis: FY2025 Standard ROIC is canonically reconstructed and bounded.
All-In ROIC and ex-goodwill diagnostics are coherent.
ROIIC is NOT_INTERPRETABLE and ROIC_TREND remains UNCLEAR due missing normalized multi-period canonical history.
Organic versus acquired return effects cannot be cleanly separated at NOPAT/capital level.
Airgas standalone current capital employed/return is not disclosed.
NovaAir purchase economics are incompletely disclosed.
DIG is recent and H1 2026 capital is affected by purchase accounting, FX and construction lags.

core_findings: Total-capex standardized FCF remained positive but softened modestly as industrial investment accelerated.
Owner Earnings is a range because maintenance/safety/renewal capex is not separately disclosed; depreciation is not mechanically substituted for maintenance capex.
H1 2026 reported cash conversion is distorted by the end of factoring; a factoring-normalized diagnostic is retained without annualization.
DIG PPA and recurring/non-recurring bridges are preserved rather than silently stripped.
open_uncertainties: Maintenance capex range remains assumption-sensitive.
reopen_triggers: Material revision to maintenance-capex evidence.
Factoring or working-capital policy changes persistently alter normalized cash conversion.
Recurring exclusion policy materially expands.

core_findings: Capital deployment combines organic industrial investment, acquisitions and dividends; investment decisions and capex are kept distinct.
DIG is economically material and raised leverage; its synergy and acquisition-return case remains unproven after a short consolidation window.
NovaAir and Airgas standalone acquisition-cohort returns are not disclosed sufficiently for clean attribution.
Biogas divestiture shows portfolio recycling, while low-carbon projects require project-specific return discipline.
open_uncertainties: DIG realized synergies/retention/margins.
NovaAir purchase economics and Airgas current cohort returns.
reopen_triggers: DIG goodwill impairment or integration shortfall.
Net debt remains elevated without corresponding cash/return improvement.
Material evidence of subsidy-dependent projects earning sub-hurdle returns.

core_findings: Chairman and CEO roles are separated; the board has substantial independence and employee representation.
Employee shareholding and broad employee capital participation create some alignment, while registered-share loyalty mechanics are shareholder distribution policy rather than operating quality.
Management has demonstrated margin/efficiency execution, but causal credit is constrained by incomplete margin attribution.
CFO continuity includes prior Airgas integration experience.
open_uncertainties: Management-specific acquisition value creation remains inseparable from price paid until Valuation and later realization.
reopen_triggers: Governance independence deterioration.
Material related-party/control change.
Repeated acquisition execution failures.

core_findings: Linde and Air Products corroborate the industry's long-term on-site model but disconfirm any claim that contract duration alone is Air Liquide-specific moat proof.
Historical/local competition evidence supports basin and distribution density as economically local mechanisms rather than relying on global market-share narratives.
Messer and Nippon Sanso show credible regional/specialty competition.
Air Products' low-carbon project charges provide a base-rate warning against equating energy-transition pipelines with attractive realized returns.
reopen_triggers: New competitor displacement evidence.
Material consolidation or regulatory change in local industrial-gas markets.

core_findings: Resilience benefits from geographic/business diversification, Healthcare exposure, contractual energy pass-through in Large Industries, strong credit ratings and broad funding access.
Post-DIG leverage is materially higher and must normalize through cash generation rather than be ignored.
Healthcare reimbursement/tender pressure, semiconductor cycles, local industrial demand, FX and supply/energy disruptions remain material.
Hydrogen/CCS projects add execution, power-price, subsidy and offtake risk; project pipeline is not treated as realized resilience or return.
reopen_triggers: Credit-rating downgrade or refinancing stress.
Material customer/project cancellation.
Healthcare reimbursement shock.
Major safety/operational incident.
